translations.text: Fixing of the mind is the binding of the mind to a place.

notes: Vyāsa: in places such as the circle of the navel, the lotus of the heart, the light in the head, the tip of the nose or the tip of the tongue, or on an outer object; the binding is by the mind's activity alone.

translations.text: Meditation is the single flow of cognition there.

notes: Vyāsa: in that place, the even stream of the cognition that rests on the object of meditation, untouched by any other cognition.

padaccheda.iast: tat eva artha-mātra-nirbhāsam svarūpa-śūnyam iva samādhiḥ
padaccheda.deva: तत् एव अर्थ-मात्र-निर्भासम् स्वरूप-शून्यम् इव समाधिः

translations.text: That same (meditation), when it shines as the object alone, as if empty of its own form, is meditative absorption.

notes: Vyāsa: when meditation shines with the form of the object meditated on and is as if empty of its own form as a cognition, because the nature of that object has entered it, it is called absorption.

translations.text: The three together, on one object, are constraint.

notes: Vyāsa: fixing, meditation and absorption, the three means, when they have one object. ‘Constraint’ (saṃyama) is the technical name of this teaching for the three.

translations.text: From the mastery of that comes the light of wisdom.

notes: Vyāsa: as constraint becomes firm-footed, the wisdom of absorption becomes clear.

translations.text: It is applied to the stages.

notes: Vyāsa: when one stage is mastered, it is applied to the next. One who has not mastered a lower stage cannot leap the next and gain constraint on the last stages; and without that, whence the light of wisdom? But one who by the Lord's grace has mastered a higher stage need not apply it to lower ones, such as knowing another's mind. As to which stage comes next, yoga itself is the teacher: ‘Yoga is to be known by yoga; yoga proceeds from yoga; he who is not careless in yoga delights long in yoga.’

translations.text: The three are inner limbs compared with the earlier ones.

notes: Vyāsa: inner limbs of absorption with cognition, compared with the five means beginning with the restraints.

translations.text: Even that is an outer limb of the seedless (absorption).

notes: Vyāsa: of the seedless yoga; because that comes about when these three are absent.

words.meaning: of the latent impressions of emergence and of cessation
in which the mind is joined to the moment of cessation

translations.text: The overpowering of the latent impressions of emergence and the appearance of those of cessation, the mind being joined to the moment of cessation, is the change of cessation.

notes: Vyāsa: the impressions of emergence are properties of the mind; they are not cognitions, so they do not cease when cognition ceases. The impressions of cessation are properties of the mind too. The first are removed and the second laid down. This alteration of impressions in the one mind, moment by moment, is the change of cessation; the mind then has only impressions left.

translations.text: Its calm flow comes from the latent impression.

notes: Vyāsa: the mind's calm flow depends on skill in the practice of the impression of cessation. When that impression is weak, it is overpowered by the impression of emergence.

words.meaning: of dispersal over all objects and of one-pointedness

translations.text: The dwindling of dispersal over all objects and the rise of one-pointedness is the mind's change of absorption.

notes: Vyāsa: both are properties of the mind. The dwindling of the one is its disappearance, the rise of the other its appearance; the mind runs through both as their bearer.

padaccheda.iast: tataḥ punaḥ śānta-uditau tulya-pratyayau cittasya ekāgratā-pariṇāmaḥ
padaccheda.deva: ततः पुनः शान्त-उदितौ तुल्य-प्रत्ययौ चित्तस्य एकाग्रता-परिणामः

words.meaning: the one quieted and the one risen

translations.text: Then again, when the cognition that has quieted and the one that has risen are alike, that is the mind's change of one-pointedness.

notes: Vyāsa: in the absorbed mind the earlier cognition quiets and the later, like it, rises; the mind in absorption runs through both, and so on again until absorption breaks.

words.meaning: in the elements and the senses
the changes of property, of temporal character and of condition

grammar.en: past passive participle m. nom. pl.

translations.text: By this are explained the changes of property, of temporal character and of condition in the elements and the senses.

notes: Vyāsa: in the mind, the overpowering of emergence and the appearance of cessation is change of property in the bearer. Change of temporal character: cessation has three characters, joined to the three paths of time; leaving the path not yet come, without ceasing to be a property, it takes the present character, where it is manifest in its own form, and is not cut off from the past and the future ones. Change of condition: in the moments of cessation its impressions are strong and those of emergence weak. So the bearer changes by properties, the properties by temporal characters, and these by conditions; the working of the guṇas does not stand for a moment without them.

Vyāsa: in truth there is one change only, for a property is nothing but the bearer's own nature, and it is the bearer's alteration that is set out by way of the property. Only the state alters, not the substance: when a gold vessel is broken and remade it is not the gold that becomes other. Another says that the bearer is nothing beyond the properties, for if it ran through them, passing unaltered through earlier and later states, it would be immovably eternal. That is no fault, because nothing absolute is held: the three worlds pass out of manifestation, since eternity is denied; having passed out they still exist, since destruction is denied; merged, they are subtle, and being subtle they are not perceived.

Vyāsa, on the objection that if every property has all three temporal characters the times are mixed: a property is present with the present character and is not cut off from the other two, as a man attached to one woman is not averse to the rest. It is not only at the present moment that a property is a property, or the mind would not have attachment as a property while anger is at work. The three characters cannot be manifest together in one manifestation; they come in turn, as what manifests each appears. The bearer does not have the three times; the properties do, and as they reach this or that condition they are spoken of as other because of the condition, not because of the substance: as one stroke is a hundred in the hundreds' place, ten in the tens' and one in the units', and as one woman is called mother, daughter and sister.

Vyāsa, on the objection that with change of condition everything would be immovably eternal, a property being future while it does not do its work, present while it does and past when it has done it: though the bearer of the qualities is eternal, the qualities crush one another in many ways. As a shape, which has a beginning and perishes, is a mere property of sound and the rest, which do not perish, so the mark (liṅga), which has a beginning and perishes, is a mere property of sattva and the other guṇas, which do not; ‘modification’ is the name for it. His example: clay, the bearer, passes from the form of a lump to that of a pot (property); the pot-form leaves the future character for the present (temporal character); the pot is new, then old, moment by moment (condition). So one change of the substance is shown in three ways. Change is the arising of another property in an abiding substance when an earlier property ceases.

words.meaning: that which runs through the quieted, the risen and the unnamed properties

translations.text: The bearer of properties is that which runs through the properties quieted, risen and not yet named.

notes: Vyāsa: a property is the bearer's own power, marked off by its fitness (for an effect). The quieted are those that have done their work and stopped (past); the risen are those at work (present); the unnamed are those to come, for everything has the nature of everything, though all do not show at once, being tied to place, time, form and cause. The bearer runs through these manifest and unmanifest properties. For one who holds that there are only properties, with nothing running through them, there could be no experience, since one cognition would not enjoy the action done by another, and no memory; and things are recognised as the same. So there is a lasting bearer.

translations.text: Difference of sequence is the cause of difference of change.

notes: Vyāsa: lest it be thought that one bearer has only one change. Powdered clay, clay as a lump, as a pot, as shards, as grains: that is a sequence; the property that comes next after a property is its sequence. There is such a sequence for property, for temporal character (future to present, present to past; the past has none), and for condition, as a new pot is seen to be old in the end. The mind's properties are of two kinds, seen (cognitions) and unseen, the latter seven, known by inference: cessation, dharma, latent impressions, change, life, movement and power.

words.meaning: from constraint on the three changes
knowledge of the past and the future

translations.text: From constraint on the three changes comes knowledge of the past and the future.

notes: Vyāsa: on the changes of property, of temporal character and of condition. Seen directly by constraint, the three changes bring knowledge of what is past and to come in them.

words.meaning: from the superimposing of each on the other
knowledge of the cries of all beings

translations.text: Word, thing and cognition are mixed because each is superimposed on the other; from constraint on their distinction comes knowledge of the cries of all beings.

notes: Vyāsa: speech has its purpose in the sounds of letters only, and hearing has for its object only a change of sound; the word is grasped by the understanding that gathers the sounds up at the end. The letters cannot exist together, and no one of them is the word; yet, limited by the convention of a meaning, ‘g’, ‘au’ and the visarga light up the thing that has a dewlap. The single appearance in the understanding of these, their sequence drawn together, is the word: one, without parts or sequence, mental. Convention is a superimposing of word and thing on each other, in the form of memory: ‘this word is this thing, this thing is this word’. So ‘cow’ the word, ‘cow’ the thing and ‘cow’ the knowledge are mixed. He who knows them apart knows all. The thing, changing by its own conditions, goes neither with the word nor with the cognition; so the word is one thing, the object another, the cognition another.

Vyāsa: each letter by itself is not the word, yet each has the nature of a word and holds the power to express everything; taking on many forms as it is paired with other letters, the earlier is fixed to a particular sense by the later and the later by the earlier. The one word, the object of one cognition and thrown out by one effort, is brought up by the cognition of the last letter; hearers, whose understanding is steeped in the latent tendencies of the beginningless use of speech, take it as a settled thing.

Vyāsa: in every word there is the power of a sentence. When ‘tree’ is said, ‘is’ is understood, for a thing meant by a word never lacks existence; and there is no action without its means, so that ‘cooks’ implies all the factors, and naming agent, instrument and object (Caitra, fire, rice) only restricts them. A single word is also found in the sense of a sentence: śrotriya, ‘he recites the Veda’; jīvati, ‘he holds the breaths’. The sense of the word is manifest in the sentence, and the word is to be separated out and analysed as naming an action or a factor; otherwise forms such as bhavati, aśvaḥ and ajāpayaḥ, alike as noun and verb, could not be analysed. So in śvetate prāsādaḥ, ‘the palace shines white’, the word means an action, and in śvetaḥ prāsādaḥ, ‘the white palace’, a factor; the thing and the cognition have both in them, and the cognition has one form with the thing only through the tie ‘this is that’, which is the convention.

words.meaning: from the direct seeing of the latent impressions

translations.text: From the direct seeing of the latent impressions comes knowledge of former births.

notes: Vyāsa: the impressions are of two kinds: latent tendencies, the causes of memory and of the afflictions; and dharma and adharma, the causes of ripening. Formed in earlier lives, they are unseen properties of the mind. They cannot be seen directly without the experience of their place, time and cause, so from seeing them comes knowledge of former births; and likewise of another's births.

Vyāsa: a story is told. The lord Jaigīṣavya, having seen his impressions, looked on the course of his births through ten great creations, and the knowledge born of discernment arose in him. Āvaṭya asked him which he had found the greater, pleasure or pain. He answered: ‘Whatever I experienced, born again and again among gods and men, I count it all as pain.’ ‘And this mastery over pradhāna, and the unsurpassed happiness of contentment?’ ‘It is unsurpassed beside the pleasure of objects; beside the happiness of soleness it is only pain.’

translations.text: (From the direct seeing) of a cognition comes knowledge of another's mind.

notes: Vyāsa: from constraint on a cognition, from seeing it directly.

padaccheda.iast: na ca tat sālambanam tasya aviṣayībhūtatvāt
padaccheda.deva: न च तत् सालम्बनम् तस्य अविषयीभूतत्वात्

words.meaning: because it has not been made the object

translations.text: But not that together with its object, because that has not been made the object (of the yogin's mind).

notes: Vyāsa: he knows the cognition as coloured by attachment; he does not know on what object it is so coloured. The object of the other's cognition is not taken as object by the yogin's mind; only the other's cognition is.

words.meaning: from constraint on the form of the body
when its power of being grasped is arrested
when it is not joined to the light of the eye

translations.text: From constraint on the form of the body, when its power of being grasped is arrested and it is not joined to the light of the eye, comes disappearance.

notes: Vyāsa: by this the disappearance of sound and the rest is also to be understood.

sanskrit.deva: सोपक्रमं निरुपक्रमं च कर्म तत्संयमादपरान्तज्ञानमरिष्टेभ्यो वा ॥ २२ ॥
sanskrit.iast: sopakramaṃ nirupakramaṃ ca karma tatsaṃyamād aparāntajñānam ariṣṭebhyo vā || 22 ||

lines.iast: sopakramaṃ nirupakramaṃ ca karma tatsaṃyamād aparāntajñānam ariṣṭebhyo vā
lines.deva: सोपक्रमं निरुपक्रमं च कर्म तत्संयमादपरान्तज्ञानमरिष्टेभ्यो वा

padaccheda.iast: sopakramam nirupakramam ca karma tat-saṃyamāt aparānta-jñānam ariṣṭebhyaḥ vā
padaccheda.deva: सोपक्रमम् निरुपक्रमम् च कर्म तत्-संयमात् अपरान्त-ज्ञानम् अरिष्टेभ्यः वा

translations.text: Action is quick or slow in its course; from constraint on it, or from portents, comes knowledge of the end.

notes: Vyāsa: the action that ripens as the span of life is of two kinds. As a wet cloth spread out dries quickly, or fire set to dry grass with wind on every side burns fast, so the quick; as the same cloth rolled up dries slowly, or fire put to a heap of grass part by part burns long, so the slow. From constraint on it comes knowledge of the end, that is, of death. Portents are of three kinds: of oneself (with ears closed he does not hear the sound in his body), of beings (he sees the men of Yama, or the departed ancestors), of the gods (he suddenly sees heaven or the perfected ones); or he sees everything reversed.

translations.text: (From constraint) on friendliness and the rest come strengths.

notes: Vyāsa: friendliness, compassion and gladness are the three cultivations (1.33). The absorption that comes from cultivating them is constraint, and from it come strengths of unfailing vigour. Towards the wicked there is indifference, which is not a cultivation; there is no absorption in it, and so no strength.

words.meaning: the strength of an elephant and the like

translations.text: (From constraint) on strengths come the strength of an elephant and the like.

notes: Vyāsa: from constraint on the strength of an elephant he has an elephant's strength; on that of Garuḍa, Garuḍa's; on that of the wind, the wind's.

words.meaning: from casting the light of direct perception
knowledge of the subtle, the hidden and the distant

translations.text: From casting the light of direct perception comes knowledge of the subtle, the hidden and the distant.

notes: Vyāsa: the luminous perception of the mind was described (1.36); the yogin casts its light on a subtle, hidden or distant thing and knows it.

translations.text: From constraint on the sun comes knowledge of the worlds.

notes: Vyāsa: he sets out the seven worlds at length: the earth-world from the Avīci hell to the top of Meru, with the six great hells and the seven nether regions; the earth of seven continents with golden Sumeru at its centre, Jambūdvīpa and its mountains and regions, and the ringed continents and seas; the mid-region of planets and stars up to the pole star; the heaven of Mahendra; the Mahar world of Prajāpati; and the threefold world of Brahmā, Jana, Tapas and Satya, each with its orders of gods. All this stands within the egg, which is a minute part of pradhāna, like a firefly in the sky. The bodiless and those merged in Prakṛti are in a state like liberation and are not placed in any world. The yogin is to see this directly by constraint on the door of the sun, and elsewhere too, until all is seen.

Vyāsa, in more detail: above Avīci are the six great hells, Mahākāla, Ambarīṣa, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Kālasūtra and Andhatāmisra, resting on earth, water, fire, wind, space and darkness, where beings are born to a long and painful life earned by their own action; then the seven nether regions from Mahātala to Pātāla. The earth is the eighth. Sumeru has peaks of silver, beryl, crystal and gold, which colour the four quarters of the sky. To its north are three mountain ranges and the regions Ramaṇaka, Hiraṇmaya and the Northern Kurus; to its south Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa and Himaśaila and the regions Harivarṣa, Kiṃpuruṣa and Bhārata; to the east Bhadrāśva, to the west Ketumāla, in the middle Ilāvṛta. Jambūdvīpa, a hundred thousand yojanas across, is ringed by the salt sea of twice its size, and then, each twice the last, by the continents Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmala, Gomedha and Puṣkara with their seas of sugar-cane juice, wine, ghee, curd, milk and sweet water, out to the Lokāloka mountains.

Vyāsa: in Mahendra's heaven live six orders of gods, who gain their ends by a wish, have the powers beginning with minuteness, live for an age and enjoy pleasures; in the Mahar world five orders, masters of the great elements, who feed on meditation and live a thousand ages; in the Jana world four, masters of the elements and senses; in the Tapas world three, masters also of the natures, of unobstructed knowledge above and unveiled knowledge below; in the Satya world four, who build no dwelling, rest in themselves, are masters of pradhāna and live as long as the creation: the Acyutas, whose pleasure is meditation with gross thought, the Śuddhanivāsas, with subtle thought, the Satyābhas, of bliss alone, and the Saṃjñāsaṃjñins, of the bare sense of ‘I am’. These seven are all worlds of Brahmā.

words.meaning: knowledge of the array of the stars

translations.text: (From constraint) on the moon comes knowledge of the array of the stars.
(From constraint) on the pole star comes knowledge of their motion.

notes: Vyāsa: and by constraint on the celestial chariots above he may know those.

words.meaning: on the circle of the navel
knowledge of the arrangement of the body

translations.text: (From constraint) on the circle of the navel comes knowledge of the arrangement of the body.

notes: Vyāsa: the three humours are wind, bile and phlegm; the seven constituents are skin, blood, flesh, sinew, bone, marrow and semen, each earlier one outside the next.

words.meaning: on the hollow of the throat
the ceasing of hunger and thirst

translations.text: (From constraint) on the hollow of the throat comes the ceasing of hunger and thirst.

notes: Vyāsa: below the tongue is the cord, below that the throat, below that the hollow.

translations.text: (From constraint) on the tortoise channel comes steadiness.

notes: Vyāsa: below the hollow, in the chest, is a channel shaped like a tortoise; by constraint on it he gains a steady state, like a snake or a lizard.

words.meaning: on the light in the head
the sight of the perfected ones

translations.text: (From constraint) on the light in the head comes the sight of the perfected ones.

notes: Vyāsa: within the skull is an opening, a shining light. The perfected ones are those who move between heaven and earth.

translations.text: Or from the intuitive knowledge, all (is known).

notes: Vyāsa: the intuitive knowledge is called the deliverer; it is the first form of the knowledge born of discernment, as the glow is of the sun at its rising. By it too the yogin knows all.

translations.text: (From constraint) on the heart comes awareness of the mind.

notes: Vyāsa: in this city of Brahman there is a small lotus, a dwelling; consciousness is there.

sanskrit.iast: sattvapuruṣayor atyantāsaṃkīrṇayoḥ pratyayāviśeṣo bhogaḥ parārthāt svārthasaṃyamāt puruṣajñānam || 35 ||

lines.iast: sattvapuruṣayor atyantāsaṃkīrṇayoḥ pratyayāviśeṣo bhogaḥ parārthāt svārthasaṃyamāt puruṣajñānam

padaccheda.iast: sattva-puruṣayoḥ atyanta-asaṃkīrṇayoḥ pratyaya-aviśeṣaḥ bhogaḥ para-arthāt sva-artha-saṃyamāt puruṣa-jñānam
padaccheda.deva: सत्त्व-पुरुषयोः अत्यन्त-असंकीर्णयोः प्रत्यय-अविशेषः भोगः पर-अर्थात् स्व-अर्थ-संयमात् पुरुष-ज्ञानम्

words.meaning: the cognition that does not distinguish
from that which is for another
from constraint on what is for itself

translations.text: Experience is the cognition that does not distinguish sattva and the Puruṣa, which are wholly unmixed; from constraint on what is for itself, apart from that which is for another, comes knowledge of the Puruṣa.

notes: Vyāsa: the sattva of the understanding, having mastered rajas and tamas, is changed into the cognition that sattva and the Puruṣa are different. The Puruṣa, pure, of the form of consciousness alone, is wholly unlike that changing sattva. The cognition of experience belongs to sattva, and since sattva is for another, it is something seen. The cognition other than it, of the form of consciousness alone, is the Puruṣa's; from constraint on that, wisdom arises whose object is the Puruṣa. The Puruṣa is not seen by that cognition, which is of the understanding; the Puruṣa himself sees the cognition that rests on himself: ‘By what should one know the knower?’
The text has parārthāt; Vyāsa glosses sattvasya parārthatvāt, and many editions print parārthatvāt.

words.meaning: intuitive knowledge and divine hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell

translations.text: From that arise intuitive knowledge and divine hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell.

notes: Vyāsa: from the intuitive, knowledge of the subtle, hidden, distant, past and future; from śrāvaṇa the hearing of divine sound; from vedana the reaching of divine touch; from ādarśa the awareness of divine form; from āsvāda of divine taste; from vārtā the knowing of divine smell. These arise constantly.

translations.text: They are obstacles in absorption, perfections in emergence.

notes: Vyāsa: arising in one whose mind is absorbed they are obstacles, being opposed to that seeing; arising in one whose mind has emerged they are perfections.

words.meaning: from the loosening of the cause of bondage

translations.text: From the loosening of the cause of bondage and from knowing the mind's movement, the mind enters another's body.

notes: Vyāsa: the restless mind is bound, that is, fixed, in the body by force of the store of action. That action, the cause of bondage, is loosened by the strength of absorption, and the knowing of the mind's movement is born of absorption too. The yogin then draws the mind out of his own body and casts it into others; the senses follow it, as bees follow the king bee.

words.meaning: from mastery of the upward breath
in water, mud, thorns and the like

translations.text: From mastery of the upward breath come non-contact with water, mud, thorns and the like, and the going up (at death).

notes: Vyāsa: life is the working of all the senses, marked by the breaths. Its action is fivefold: prāṇa moves through mouth and nose and works as far as the heart; samāna, which carries evenly, as far as the navel; apāna, which carries away, as far as the soles; udāna, which carries up, as far as the head; vyāna pervades. Prāṇa is the chief. The going up at the time of death he gains at his own command.

words.meaning: from mastery of the even breath

translations.text: From mastery of the even breath comes blazing.

notes: Vyāsa: he who has mastered samāna fans the fire (of the body) and blazes.

translations.text: From constraint on the relation of hearing and space comes divine hearing.

notes: Vyāsa: space is the ground of all organs of hearing and of all sounds. It is known as unobstructing and all-pervading. Hearing is inferred from the grasping of sound: of a deaf man and one not deaf, one grasps sound and the other does not.

words.meaning: from coalescence with light things such as cotton

translations.text: From constraint on the relation of the body and space, or from coalescence with light things such as cotton, comes moving through space.

notes: Vyāsa: where the body is there is space, which gives it room. Mastering that relation, or coalescing with light things down to the atom, he becomes light: he walks on water, then on a spider's thread, then on rays of light, and then moves through space at will.

sanskrit.iast: bahir akalpitā vṛttir mahāvidehā tataḥ prakāśāvaraṇakṣayaḥ || 43 ||

lines.iast: bahir akalpitā vṛttir mahāvidehā tataḥ prakāśāvaraṇakṣayaḥ

padaccheda.iast: bahiḥ akalpitā vṛttiḥ mahā-videhā tataḥ prakāśa-āvaraṇa-kṣayaḥ
padaccheda.deva: बहिः अकल्पिता वृत्तिः महा-विदेहा ततः प्रकाश-आवरण-क्षयः

words.meaning: the wasting away of the covering of the light

translations.text: The activity (of the mind) outside (the body) that is not imagined is the great bodiless; from that the covering of the light wastes away.

notes: Vyāsa: the mind's gaining an activity outside the body is the fixing called ‘bodiless’. If the mind stays in the body and only its activity is outside, it is imagined; if the mind itself is outside, independent of the body, it is not imagined. By the first they achieve the second, the great bodiless, by which yogins enter other bodies. From it the covering of the sattva of the understanding, namely affliction, action and its ripening, rooted in rajas and tamas, wastes away.

words.meaning: from constraint on the gross, the own nature, the subtle, the inherent and the purposefulness

translations.text: From constraint on their gross form, own nature, subtle form, inherence and purposefulness comes mastery of the elements.

notes: Vyāsa: the five forms of the elements. The gross: the particulars, sound and the rest, of earth and the others, with shape and other properties. The own nature: the general character of each: solidity is earth, moisture water, heat fire, motion air, going everywhere space. A substance is an aggregate of the general and the particular whose parts do not exist apart, as Patañjali says. The subtle: the subtle element, the cause of the element. The inherent: the guṇas, whose nature is illumination, activity and inertia. Purposefulness: their being for experience and liberation. He who has mastered the five forms masters the elements; their natures follow his intention as cows follow their calves.

Vyāsa, on what a substance is: of the general character the particulars, sound and the rest, are the differences; things of one class differ only by their properties. A group is of two kinds. In one the parts are not named apart: a body, a tree, a herd, a wood. In the other the word names the parts: ‘gods and men’, the gods one part of the group and men the other. It may be spoken of with or without the difference: ‘a wood of mangoes’ or ‘a mango-wood’. Again a group has parts that exist apart, as a wood or an assembly, or parts that do not, as a body, a tree or an atom; the second kind is a substance. The subtle form is the subtle element; one part of it is the atom, itself an aggregate of the general and the particular whose parts do not exist apart. The guṇas, which follow the nature of their effects, are the inherent; purposefulness inheres in the guṇas, and the guṇas in the subtle elements, the elements and what is made of them, so that everything has a purpose. From constraint on each form comes the sight of that form as it is, and mastery of it.

words.meaning: the appearance of minuteness and the rest
the not being obstructed by their properties

translations.text: From that come the appearance of minuteness and the rest, excellence of the body, and its not being obstructed by their properties.

notes: Vyāsa: the eight lordly powers: minuteness; lightness; greatness; reach (he touches the moon with a fingertip); freedom of will (he dives into the earth as into water); control over the elements and their products; lordship over their arising, ending and arrangement; and the fulfilment of whatever he intends. Though able, he does not overturn the order of things, because of the intention of another, perfected before him, whose will is fulfilled. Not obstructed: earth does not stop him by its solidity, he enters even a rock; water does not wet him, fire does not burn him, wind does not move him; even in open space he is hidden.

words.meaning: beauty, grace, strength and the firmness of a thunderbolt

translations.text: Excellence of the body is beauty, grace, strength and the firmness of a thunderbolt.

words.meaning: from constraint on the grasping, the own nature, the sense of ‘I am’, the inherent and the purposefulness

translations.text: From constraint on their grasping, own nature, sense of ‘I am’, inherence and purposefulness comes mastery of the senses.

notes: Vyāsa: the five forms of the senses. Grasping: their activity towards sound and the rest. Own nature: the sense as a substance, an aggregate of the general and the particular of the luminous sattva of the understanding. The third: the ego, marked by the sense of ‘I am’, of which the senses are particulars. The fourth: the guṇas, of which the senses with the ego are a change. The fifth: their being for the Puruṣa's purpose.

words.meaning: swiftness like that of the mind
the state of being without the organs

translations.text: From that come swiftness like that of the mind, working without the organs, and mastery of pradhāna.

notes: Vyāsa: the body's gaining unsurpassed speed; the senses' working without the body, at the place, time and object wished for; and control over all Prakṛti and its modifications. These three perfections are called ‘honey-faced’.

words.meaning: of one who has only the vision of the difference of sattva and the Puruṣa

translations.text: One who has only the vision of the difference of sattva and the Puruṣa has lordship over all states and knowledge of all.

notes: Vyāsa: when the sattva of the understanding, washed of rajas and tamas, rests in that vision alone. Lordship: the guṇas, which are everything, stand before their owner, the knower of the field, as all that is to be seen. Knowledge of all: the knowledge born of discernment, without sequence, of the guṇas as quieted, risen and unnamed properties. This perfection is called ‘the sorrowless’.

words.meaning: when the seeds of the faults waste away

translations.text: From dispassion even towards that, when the seeds of the faults waste away, there is soleness.

notes: Vyāsa: when he sees that this cognition of discernment is a property of sattva, that sattva is among the things to be avoided, and that the Puruṣa is changeless, pure and other than sattva, he turns from it. The seeds of the afflictions, like burnt rice seeds, set together with the mind, and the Puruṣa no longer suffers the three kinds of distress. Soleness is the Puruṣa's final separation from the guṇas; then he is the power of consciousness alone, resting in his own nature.

words.meaning: when invited by those in high places
not giving way to attachment or pride

translations.text: When invited by those in high places, he should not give way to attachment or pride, because the unwished would follow again.

notes: Vyāsa: yogins are of four kinds: the beginner, in whom the light has just begun; one at the honeyed stage, whose wisdom is truth-bearing; one of the light of wisdom, who has mastered the elements and the senses; and one gone beyond what is to be cultivated, for whom only the dissolving of the mind remains. The gods invite the one at the honeyed stage: ‘Sit here, enjoy here; here are pleasures, maidens, the elixir against age and death, a chariot of the sky, wish-granting trees.’ Let him reflect on the faults of attachment: ‘Burning on the coals of the cycle of birth and death, I have somehow found the lamp of yoga; these winds of sense objects are its enemies. How should I, having found the light, be cheated by this mirage?’ Nor should he feel pride that even the gods seek him; from pride he will think himself secure, carelessness will find its opening and rouse the afflictions.

Vyāsa: the third kind of yogin has made safe what he has already cultivated and has the means for what is still to be done; for the fourth, wisdom has seven final stages (2.27). The one who is invited should say, with his mind made up: ‘Fare you well, objects that are like dreams and are sought by pitiable men’, and cultivate absorption. Proud, he would not think of himself as seized by the hair by death. When he gives way to neither attachment nor pride, what he has cultivated grows firm and what is still to be cultivated comes before him.

words.meaning: on the moment and its sequence

translations.text: From constraint on the moment and its sequence comes the knowledge born of discernment.

notes: Vyāsa: as the atom is the smallest limit of substance, the moment is the smallest limit of time: the time in which a moving atom leaves one point and reaches the next. The unbroken flow of moments is their sequence. There is no real collection of moments; hours, days and nights are collections made by the understanding. Time, empty of reality, follows from the knowledge of words. Two moments do not exist together; only the present moment is. In that one moment the whole world undergoes change.

words.meaning: since their difference is not determined

translations.text: From that comes the ascertainment of two things that are alike, their difference not being determined by kind, mark or place.

notes: Vyāsa: difference is known by kind (a cow, a mare), by mark (the black-eyed cow, the lucky cow), or by place (two myrobalan fruits, one in front, one behind). But if, while the knower looks away, the one is put in the place of the other, they cannot be told apart by these. The knowledge born of discernment tells them apart: the place joined with the moment of the one differs from that of the other. So even of two atoms the yogin has the cognition of their difference.

sanskrit.iast: tārakaṃ sarvaviṣayaṃ sarvathāviṣayam akramaṃ ceti vivekajaṃ jñānam || 54 ||

padaccheda.iast: tārakam sarva-viṣayam sarvathā-viṣayam akramam ca iti viveka-jam jñānam
padaccheda.deva: तारकम् सर्व-विषयम् सर्वथा-विषयम् अक्रमम् च इति विवेक-जम् ज्ञानम्

words.meaning: having its object in every way

translations.text: The knowledge born of discernment is the deliverer; it has all for its object, in every way, and is without sequence.

notes: Vyāsa: ‘the deliverer’: it rises from one's own intuition, not from teaching. ‘All for its object’: nothing is outside it. ‘In every way’: it knows all, past, future and present, with all their aspects. ‘Without sequence’: it grasps all in a single moment.

translations.text: When the purity of sattva and of the Puruṣa is equal, there is soleness.

notes: Vyāsa: when the sattva of the understanding, washed of rajas and tamas, its only task the cognition that the Puruṣa is other, the seeds of affliction burnt, has become as if like the Puruṣa in purity; and the Puruṣa's purity is the absence of the experience ascribed to him. In this state there is soleness, whether or not he has the powers and the knowledge born of discernment; for one whose seeds of affliction are burnt needs nothing further for knowledge. In truth non-seeing ceases through knowledge; then there are no afflictions, and so no ripening of action. The Puruṣa is then the light of his own nature alone, stainless and sole.
